dryRun.title: Looking up dog.toString()
dryRun.note: Every object has a hidden link ([[Prototype]]) to another object. Reading a property walks that chain until it finds it or reaches null. Writing a property always creates an own property.

think.q:
const base = { greet() { return 'hi ' + this.name } }
const u = Object.create(base)
u.name = 'A'
console.log(u.greet(), Object.hasOwn(u, 'greet'))
why: greet is found on the prototype; this is still u (left of the dot). It is not an own property.

think.q:
const proto = { list: [] }
const a = Object.create(proto), b = Object.create(proto)
a.list.push(1)
console.log(b.list.length)
why: a.list reads the shared array from the prototype and mutates it. Shared mutable state on a prototype is a classic bug.

think.q:
const proto = { n: 1 }
const o = Object.create(proto)
o.n = 2
console.log(o.n, proto.n)
why: Assignment creates an own property on o that shadows the prototype one. The prototype is unchanged.

think.q: console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf([]) === Array.prototype, Object.getPrototypeOf(Array.prototype) === Object.prototype, Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype))
why: [] → Array.prototype → Object.prototype → null. That is why arrays have both map and hasOwnProperty.
think.exec: console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf([]) === Array.prototype, Object.getPrototypeOf(Array.prototype) === Object.prototype, Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype))

think.q: How do you safely check if an object itself (not its prototype) has a key?
why: in walks the chain. A value check fails for keys holding undefined.

try.task: Write protoChain(obj): return the list of prototypes of obj, nearest first, ending before null. Then write findOwner(obj, key): return the object in the chain (obj itself or a prototype) that owns key, or null.
try.hint: Loop with Object.getPrototypeOf until null; check Object.hasOwn at each step.

checks.verify: const c = protoChain([]); assert(c.length === 2 && c[0] === Array.prototype && c[1] === Object.prototype, "chain")
assert(protoChain(Object.create(null)).length === 0, "null proto")

checks.t: findOwner finds own and inherited keys
checks.verify: const a = [1]; assert(findOwner(a, "0") === a && findOwner(a, "map") === Array.prototype && findOwner(a, "nope") === null, "owner")

takeaway.key: Reads walk the prototype chain; writes create own properties. Never put mutable shared data on a prototype.
mistakes: Using in when you meant "own property".
Shared arrays/objects on a prototype, mutated through one instance.

dryRun.title: new User("A")
rows: calls User with this = that object
returns the object, unless User returns another object
dryRun.note: Four steps. Forgetting new on an old-style constructor runs it with the wrong this. Classes protect you: calling a class without new throws.

think.q:
function User(n) { this.n = n }
User.prototype.hi = function () { return 'hi ' + this.n }
console.log(new User('A').hi())
why: The new object is linked to User.prototype, so it finds hi; this inside is the new object.

think.q:
function A() { this.x = 1; return { y: 2 } }
function B() { this.x = 1; return 5 }
console.log(new A().x, new B().x)
why: Returning an object replaces the new object. Returning a primitive is ignored.

think.q:
function P() {}
const p = new P()
console.log(p instanceof P, p.constructor === P, Object.getPrototypeOf(p) === P.prototype)
why: All three follow from step 2: the new object is linked to P.prototype, whose constructor points back to P.

think.q:
class C {}
try { C() } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: Classes must be called with new.
think.exec:
class C {}
try { C() } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }

think.q: Can an arrow function be used with new?
opts: No: arrows have no prototype and no own this, so new throws a TypeError
Only if it returns an object
why: Constructors need their own this and a prototype.

try.task: Implement myNew(Ctor, ...args) that does what new does (all 4 steps), without using new.
try.hint: Object.create(Ctor.prototype), then Ctor.apply(obj, args); if the result is an object (or function) return it, else obj.

checks.t: sets fields and links the prototype
checks.verify: function P(n) { this.n = n }; P.prototype.get = function () { return this.n }; const p = myNew(P, 4); assert(p.n === 4 && p.get() === 4 && p instanceof P, "basic")
function A() { this.x = 1; return { y: 2 } }; assert(myNew(A).y === 2 && myNew(A).x === undefined, "object return")

checks.t: a primitive return value is ignored
checks.verify: function B() { this.x = 1; return 5 }; assert(myNew(B).x === 1, "primitive return")

takeaway.key: new = create object, link to Ctor.prototype, run Ctor with this, return it (unless Ctor returns an object).
mistakes: Calling an old-style constructor without new.
Returning an object from a constructor by accident.

dryRun.title: class Counter { #n = 0; static made = 0; inc() {} get value() {} }
dryRun.note: A class is mostly syntax over constructor functions and prototypes, plus real extras: #private fields, static members, getters/setters, and it must be called with new.

think.q:
class C { #secret = 1; reveal() { return this.#secret } }
const c = new C()
console.log(c.reveal(), c.secret, Object.keys(c).length)
why: #secret is truly private: not a normal property, not in keys.

think.q:
class A { static count = 0; constructor() { A.count++ } }
new A(); new A()
console.log(A.count, new A().count)
why: Static members live on the class. Instances do not see them. (The third new A runs after A.count is read.)

think.q:
class T { constructor() { this.v = 2 } get double() { return this.v * 2 } }
const t = new T()
t.v = 5
console.log(t.double, typeof T.prototype.double)
why: A getter runs on every read, so it sees the new v. Reading it on the prototype runs it with this = prototype (v undefined) → NaN → typeof "number".

think.q:
class K { method() {} }
console.log(typeof K, Object.hasOwn(new K(), 'method'))
why: A class is a function. Methods live on the prototype, not on each instance.
think.exec:
class K { method() {} }
console.log(typeof K, Object.hasOwn(new K(), 'method'))

think.q: class B { handle = () => this.x }. What is the trade-off of this arrow field?
opts: It is shared on the prototype
this is always the instance (safe as a callback), but every instance gets its own copy of the function
why: Prototype methods are shared; arrow fields are per instance.

try.task: Write a class Stack with a private #items array, methods push(x) (returns the size), pop(), peek(), a getter size, and a static from(array).
try.hint: Use #items = []; static from creates a Stack and pushes each item.

checks.verify: const s = new Stack(); s.push(1); assert(s.push(2) === 2 && s.peek() === 2 && s.pop() === 2 && s.size === 1, "basic")
const s = Stack.from([1, 2, 3]); assert(s instanceof Stack && s.size === 3 && s.peek() === 3, "from")
const s = Stack.from([1]); assert(Object.keys(s).length === 0 && s.items === undefined && typeof s.size === "number", "private")

takeaway.key: Classes give private #fields, static members and getters on top of prototypes. Methods are shared; arrow fields are per instance.
mistakes: Thinking _underscore fields are private.
Expecting instances to see static members.

dryRun.title: class Dog extends Animal { constructor(n) { super(n); this.kind = "dog" } }
dryRun.note: extends links two prototype chains. In a subclass constructor you must call super() before using this. super.method() calls the parent version.

think.q:
class A { hi() { return 'A' } }
class B extends A { hi() { return 'B' + super.hi() } }
console.log(new B().hi())
why: B overrides hi and calls the parent with super.hi().

think.q:
class A { constructor() { this.x = 1 } }
class B extends A { constructor() { try { this.y = 2 } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) } super() } }
new B()
why: this does not exist in a derived constructor until super() runs.

think.q:
class A {}
class B extends A {}
const b = new B()
console.log(b instanceof A, Object.getPrototypeOf(B) === A)
why: Instances chain through the prototypes, and the classes themselves are chained too (so static methods are inherited).

think.q:
class A { static make() { return new this() } }
class B extends A {}
console.log(B.make() instanceof B)
why: Static methods are inherited, and this inside a static method is the class it was called on, B.

think.q: A Bird class gets fly(). Then Penguin extends Bird but cannot fly. What does this tell you?
opts: Add an empty fly() to Penguin
The hierarchy is wrong: prefer composing abilities over deep inheritance
why: Inheritance is an "is-a" promise. When subclasses must break parent behaviour, compose instead (next: mixins).

try.task: Create class Shape { area() { return 0 } describe() { return `${this.constructor.name} with area ${this.area()}` } }, and subclasses Rect(w, h) and Square(side) where Square extends Rect.
try.hint: Square's constructor calls super(side, side). Only Rect needs its own area().

checks.verify: assert(new Rect(2, 5).describe() === "Rect with area 10", "rect")
assert(new Square(3).describe() === "Square with area 9", "square")
const s = new Square(1); assert(s instanceof Rect && s instanceof Shape && !Object.hasOwn(Square.prototype, "area"), "chain")

takeaway.key: extends chains prototypes; call super() before this; override and call super.method(). Keep hierarchies shallow.
mistakes: Using this before super() in a subclass constructor.
Deep hierarchies where children have to undo parent behaviour.

problems.name: Check if Object Instance of Class

dryRun.title: Object.freeze vs Object.seal vs Object.preventExtensions
dryRun.note: All three are shallow. In strict mode a blocked change throws; in sloppy mode it fails silently. Object.assign copies own enumerable properties; Object.create(proto) makes an object with a chosen prototype.

think.q:
'use strict'
const o = Object.freeze({ a: 1, inner: { b: 1 } })
try { o.a = 2 } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
o.inner.b = 2
console.log(o.inner.b)
why: Changing a frozen property throws in strict mode. The nested object is not frozen.

think.q:
const t = { a: 1 }
const r = Object.assign(t, { b: 2 }, { a: 3 })
console.log(r === t, t.a, t.b)
why: assign mutates and returns the target. Later sources win.

think.q:
const o = Object.create(null)
o.x = 1
console.log(typeof o.toString, 'x' in o)
why: An object with a null prototype has no toString, hasOwnProperty, etc. Useful as a pure dictionary.

think.q:
const o = Object.seal({ a: 1 })
o.a = 5; o.b = 1; delete o.a
console.log(o.a, o.b)
why: Sealed: values can change, but adding and deleting silently fail (sloppy mode).

think.q: Object.assign({}, src) where src has a getter get now(). What ends up in the copy?
opts: A plain value: the getter is called once and its result copied
why: assign reads values. To copy getters use Object.defineProperties with getOwnPropertyDescriptors.

try.task: Write deepFreeze(obj): freeze the object and every nested object/array (any depth). Return obj.
examples: const o = deepFreeze({ a: { b: 1 } }); Object.isFrozen(o.a)  // true
try.hint: Freeze, then recurse into values that are objects and not already frozen.

checks.verify: const o = { a: 1 }; deepFreeze(o); assert(Object.isFrozen(o), "top")

checks.t: nested objects and arrays are frozen
checks.verify: const o = deepFreeze({ a: { b: { c: [1, { d: 1 }] } } }); assert(Object.isFrozen(o.a.b) && Object.isFrozen(o.a.b.c) && Object.isFrozen(o.a.b.c[1]), "nested")
const o = {}; assert(deepFreeze(o) === o, "same")

takeaway.key: freeze/seal/preventExtensions are shallow. assign copies own enumerable values (getters run). Object.create(null) gives a clean dictionary.
mistakes: Thinking freeze is deep.
Not noticing silent failures in sloppy mode.

dryRun.title: Composing abilities instead of a class tree
dryRun.note: Composition: build objects from small behaviour pieces (functions that add methods). It avoids the "Penguin extends Bird but cannot fly" problem of inheritance.

think.q:
const canSwim = (o) => ({ ...o, swim: () => o.name + ' swims' })
const canWalk = (o) => ({ ...o, walk: () => o.name + ' walks' })
const penguin = canWalk(canSwim({ name: 'P' }))
console.log(penguin.swim(), typeof penguin.fly)
why: Only the abilities you compose are present.

think.q:
const Serializable = (Base) => class extends Base { toJSON() { return { type: this.constructor.name } } }
class User {}
class Admin extends Serializable(User) {}
console.log(JSON.stringify(new Admin()), new Admin() instanceof User)
why: A class mixin is a function that takes a base class and returns a subclass. instanceof still works through the chain.

think.q:
const a = { hi() { return 'a' } }, b = { hi() { return 'b' } }
console.log(Object.assign({}, a, b).hi())
why: With Object.assign mixins, the last one wins on a name clash. Clashes are the main risk.
think.exec:
const a = { hi() { return 'a' } }, b = { hi() { return 'b' } }
console.log(Object.assign({}, a, b).hi())

think.q:
const counter = () => { let n = 0; return { inc: () => ++n } }
const o = { ...counter(), ...counter() }
o.inc()
console.log(o.inc())
why: The second counter's inc overwrites the first. Each call of counter() has its own n; o keeps only the last one.

think.q: When is inheritance still the better choice?
opts: When objects have more than 3 methods
A true, stable "is-a" relationship with shared behaviour, like Error → ValidationError
why: Composition is the default for mixing abilities; inheritance fits small, stable hierarchies.

try.task: Write withEvents(obj) that returns a new object with obj's properties plus on(name, fn) and emit(name, ...args); listeners are private per object.
examples: const u = withEvents({ name: "a" }); u.on("x", (v) => v); u.emit("x", 1)
try.hint: Keep a Map of listeners in a closure; spread obj into the result.

checks.verify: assert(withEvents({ name: "a" }).name === "a", "props")
const u = withEvents({}); let got = []; u.on("x", (a, b) => got.push(a + b)); u.on("x", () => got.push("2nd")); u.emit("x", 1, 2); assert(got.join() === "3,2nd", "emit")
const a = withEvents({}), b = withEvents({}); let n = 0; a.on("x", () => n++); b.emit("x"); assert(n === 0, "shared listeners")

takeaway.key: Compose small behaviours into objects; inherit only for real is-a. Watch name clashes when mixing.
mistakes: Deep inheritance for "can do" abilities.
Two mixins defining the same method silently.

dryRun.title: Symbols as keys
dryRun.note: A Symbol is a unique, non-string key. Two symbols are never equal, even with the same description. Well-known symbols like Symbol.iterator and Symbol.toPrimitive let you hook into language behaviour.

think.q: console.log(Symbol('a') === Symbol('a'), Symbol.for('a') === Symbol.for('a'))
why: Symbol() always makes a new one. Symbol.for uses a global registry, so the same key gives the same symbol.
think.exec: console.log(Symbol('a') === Symbol('a'), Symbol.for('a') === Symbol.for('a'))

think.q:
const id = Symbol('id')
const u = { name: 'A', [id]: 7 }
console.log(Object.keys(u).length, JSON.stringify(u), u[id])
why: Symbol keys are hidden from keys and JSON, but you can read them if you have the symbol.

think.q:
const money = { amount: 5, [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) { return hint === 'number' ? this.amount : '₹' + this.amount } }
console.log(+money, `${money}`)
why: toPrimitive receives a hint: "number" for unary +, "string" for template literals.
think.exec:
const money = { amount: 5, [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) { return hint === 'number' ? this.amount : '₹' + this.amount } }
console.log(+money, `${money}`)

think.q:
class Temp { static [Symbol.hasInstance](x) { return typeof x === 'number' } }
console.log(5 instanceof Temp)
why: Symbol.hasInstance customises instanceof. Rarely needed, but it shows how well-known symbols work.
think.exec:
class Temp { static [Symbol.hasInstance](x) { return typeof x === 'number' } }
console.log(5 instanceof Temp)

think.q: What is a good everyday use of a Symbol?
opts: A hidden metadata key on objects you do not own, which cannot clash with their own keys
why: A symbol key can never collide with a library's string keys.

try.task: Write makeMoney(amount, currency) returning an object that works with +m (the number), `${m}` (like "5.00 INR") and m + 1 (a number), using Symbol.toPrimitive.
try.hint: hint is "number", "string" or "default"; return the number for "number" and "default".

checks.verify: assert(+makeMoney(5, "INR") === 5, "number")
assert(`${makeMoney(5, "INR")}` === "5.00 INR", "string")
assert(makeMoney(5, "INR") + 1 === 6 && makeMoney(2, "X") * 3 === 6, "default")

takeaway.key: Symbols are unique keys, hidden from keys/JSON. Well-known symbols (iterator, toPrimitive, hasInstance) hook into the language.
mistakes: Expecting two Symbol("x") to be equal.
Expecting symbol-keyed data to survive JSON.stringify.

dryRun.title: for (const x of range(1, 3))
dryRun.note: An object is iterable if it has a [Symbol.iterator]() method returning an iterator: an object with next() that returns { value, done }. for…of, spread and destructuring all use this protocol.

think.q:
const it = [10, 20][Symbol.iterator]()
console.log(JSON.stringify([it.next(), it.next(), it.next()]))
why: The third call returns { value: undefined, done: true }; JSON drops undefined values, so it shows {"done":true}.
think.exec:
const it = [10, 20][Symbol.iterator]()
console.log(JSON.stringify([it.next(), it.next(), it.next()]))

think.q:
const obj = { a: 1 }
try { for (const x of obj) {} } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: Plain objects are not iterable. Use Object.entries(obj) or for…in.
think.exec:
const obj = { a: 1 }
try { for (const x of obj) {} } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }

think.q: console.log([...'héllo'].length, [...new Set('aab')].join(''))
why: Strings and Sets are iterable. Spread uses the iterator.
think.exec: console.log([...'héllo'].length, [...new Set('aab')].join(''))

think.q:
const r = { from: 1, to: 3, [Symbol.iterator]() { let c = this.from, t = this.to; return { next: () => c <= t ? { value: c++, done: false } : { value: undefined, done: true } } } }
console.log([...r].join(','), Math.max(...r))
why: A hand-written iterable works with spread and with function arguments.
think.exec:
const r = { from: 1, to: 3, [Symbol.iterator]() { let c = this.from, t = this.to; return { next: () => c <= t ? { value: c++, done: false } : { value: undefined, done: true } } } }
console.log([...r].join(','), Math.max(...r))

think.q: Why is the iterator protocol "lazy"?
opts: Values are produced one by one when next() is called, so a sequence can even be infinite
why: Nothing is computed until someone asks for the next value.

try.task: Make range(start, end, step = 1) return an iterable object (not an array) so that [...range(1, 5)] is [1, 2, 3, 4] (end excluded) and it can be iterated more than once.
try.hint: Return { [Symbol.iterator]() { let c = start; return { next() {...} } } }. A fresh counter per call makes it reusable.

checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify([...range(1, 5)]) === "[1,2,3,4]" && JSON.stringify([...range(0, 10, 3)]) === "[0,3,6,9]", "values")
assert(!Array.isArray(range(0, 2)) && typeof range(0, 2)[Symbol.iterator] === "function", "iterable")
const r = range(0, 3); assert([...r].length === 3 && [...r].length === 3, "reusable")

takeaway.key: Iterable = has [Symbol.iterator]() returning { next() → { value, done } }. for…of, spread and destructuring use it.
mistakes: for…of on a plain object.
Returning the same exhausted iterator every time, so the object can be looped only once.

dryRun.title: function* g() { const x = yield 1; yield x * 2 }
dryRun.note: A generator function (function*) returns an iterator. Each yield pauses it; next(v) resumes it and v becomes the value of that yield. It is the easiest way to write an iterable.

think.q:
function* g() { console.log('start'); yield 1; yield 2 }
const it = g()
console.log('created')
console.log(it.next().value)
why: Calling a generator runs nothing. The body starts at the first next().

think.q:
function* nat() { let n = 1; while (true) yield n++ }
const first3 = []
for (const n of nat()) { if (n > 3) break; first3.push(n) }
console.log(first3.join(''))
why: An infinite generator is fine: values are made on demand and break stops it.

think.q:
function* g() { const a = yield 'q1'; const b = yield 'q2'; return a + b }
const it = g()
it.next(); it.next(2)
console.log(it.next(3).value)
why: The first next() starts it (its argument is ignored). 2 goes into a, 3 into b, return gives 5.

think.q:
function* inner() { yield 'a'; yield 'b' }
function* outer() { yield 1; yield* inner(); yield 2 }
console.log([...outer()].join(''))
why: yield* delegates to another iterable.

think.q: What does a return 9 inside a generator do in a for…of loop?
opts: for…of receives 9 as the last item
It ends the generator; for…of ignores the returned value
why: The return value appears only as { value: 9, done: true } from next().

try.task: Write a generator flattenDeep(arr) that yields every non-array value of a nested array, in order, at any depth.
try.hint: For each item: if it is an array, yield* flattenDeep(item); else yield it.

checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify([...flattenDeep([1, [2, [3, [4]]]])]) === "[1,2,3,4]", "deep")
assert(JSON.stringify([...flattenDeep([[], [[]], 5])]) === "[5]", "empty")
const it = flattenDeep([1, 2]); assert(typeof it.next === "function" && it.next().value === 1, "lazy")

takeaway.key: function* returns a pausable iterator: yield gives a value out, next(v) sends one in, yield* delegates.
mistakes: Expecting the body to run when you call the generator.
Forgetting that the first next() argument is ignored.

dryRun.title: new Proxy(target, { get, set })
dryRun.note: A Proxy intercepts basic operations on an object. Reflect has a method for each trap that does the default behaviour, so a trap can add logic and then forward with Reflect.set(...arguments). Vue 3 reactivity is built on this.

think.q:
const p = new Proxy({}, { get: (t, k) => k in t ? t[k] : 'missing:' + String(k) })
p.a = 1
console.log(p.a, p.b)
why: The get trap returns a default for unknown keys. Set has no trap, so it goes straight to the target.

think.q:
const log = []
const p = new Proxy({}, { set(t, k, v) { log.push(k); return Reflect.set(t, k, v) } })
p.x = 1; p.y = 2
console.log(log.join(), JSON.stringify(p))
why: The trap logs and then forwards to Reflect.set, so the values really land on the target.
think.exec:
const log = []
const p = new Proxy({}, { set(t, k, v) { log.push(k); return Reflect.set(t, k, v) } })
p.x = 1; p.y = 2
console.log(log.join(), JSON.stringify(p))

think.q:
'use strict'
const p = new Proxy({}, { set: () => false })
try { p.a = 1 } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: A set trap returning false means "refused". In strict mode that throws a TypeError.

think.q:
const target = { n: 1 }
const p = new Proxy(target, {})
p.n = 2
console.log(target.n, p === target)
why: An empty handler forwards everything to the target. The proxy is a different object.

think.q: Which is a real use of Proxy?
opts: Validation or change tracking on an object without changing the code that uses it
why: Reactivity (Vue), validation, logging, default values, negative array indexes.

try.task: Write validated(schema): return a Proxy over an empty object where setting a key not in schema throws Error("unknown key"), and setting a value of the wrong typeof throws TypeError. Valid sets work normally.
examples: const u = validated({ age: "number" }); u.age = 3; u.age  // 3
try.hint: In the set trap: check k in schema, then typeof v === schema[k], then return Reflect.set(t, k, v).

checks.verify: const u = validated({ age: "number", name: "string" }); u.age = 3; u.name = "a"; assert(u.age === 3 && u.name === "a", "valid")
const u = validated({ age: "number" }); let e; try { u.age = "3" } catch (x) { e = x }; assert(e instanceof TypeError && u.age === undefined, "type")
const u = validated({ age: "number" }); let e; try { u.zzz = 1 } catch (x) { e = x }; assert(e && e.message === "unknown key", "unknown")

takeaway.key: Proxy intercepts get/set/has/delete…; Reflect does the default for each. Forward with Reflect inside traps.
mistakes: Forgetting to return true (or Reflect.set) from a set trap.
Using proxies on hot paths without measuring: they are slower.
